method: Models Linux's ephemeral source-port pool as a Little's-law queue. Each completed outbound connection holds one source port for the TIME_WAIT duration (2 x MSL, 60 s by default), so a steady rate of r new connections per second pins about r x TIME_WAIT ports at once; the port count is rounded up because ports are indivisible. Ports needed per source IP = ceil(r x TIME_WAIT) + concurrent sockets. The pool size is end - start + 1 from the configured range (Linux defaults to net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 32768 60999; Windows uses 49152-65535). Utilisation = needed / pool, shown to one decimal place. The safe sustained rate per IP = (pool - concurrent sockets) / TIME_WAIT, floored at zero, which is the rate at which the pool is exactly full; the churn ceiling = pool / TIME_WAIT is the same figure with no long-lived sockets. Status is evaluated on the unrounded ratio: exhausted when needed >= pool (the next connection fails with EADDRNOTAVAIL), tight at 85 % or more, watch at 70 % or more, otherwise healthy. Aggregate figures multiply the per-IP pool, demand and connection rate by the source IP count, because NAT gateways and proxies draw from one pool per source address. Inputs are validated as whole numbers (ports 1-65,535, TIME_WAIT 1-3,600 s, sockets 0-1,000,000, source IPs 1-10,000) or numbers with up to three decimals for the connection rate, with the end port required to be at least the start port. Pure arithmetic over the entered values: no storage, no network access, no host inspection.
